title: Replace MD5 with SHA-256 in JFrog Xray ID generation
description:
CRITICAL security finding: JFrog Xray converter uses crypto/md5 (Go) and createHash('md5') from Node crypto (TS) for generating fallback requirement IDs from vulnerability summaries. MD5 is collision-prone — crafted inputs with colliding hashes could silently merge unrelated findings. Also violates the no-crypto-import rule for TS converters.

Fix: Replace MD5 with truncated SHA-256 in both Go and TS. Use shared.InputChecksum pattern (Go) or sha256() from hdf-utilities (TS). Coordinate both implementations for parity.

Files:
- hdf-converters/converters/jfrog-xray-to-hdf/go/converter.go (line 4, 76-87)
- hdf-converters/converters/jfrog-xray-to-hdf/typescript/converter.ts (line 2, 71)
close_reason: MD5 replaced with SHA-256 in both Go and TS. Commit 7ddb063.

title: Research SAF CLI / heimdall2 aws-config converter design for input format and field mapping
description:
Both heimdall2 and SAF CLI aws-config converters use live AWS SDK calls (credentials + region), not a static file. Our converter must be file-based. Determine:

1. What static export format should users generate? Options:
   a. `aws configservice describe-config-rules` + `get-compliance-details-by-config-rule` merged into a combined JSON
   b. Just EvaluationResults (current approach) with rule metadata in a separate file
   c. A custom combined format we define

2. Fix field mapping gaps vs reference implementation:
   - Control ID: use ConfigRuleId (e.g. 'config-rule-7hytm9'), not ConfigRuleName
   - Title: '{accountId} - {ConfigRuleName}' (account ID from ConfigRuleArn)
   - NIST lookup: use Source.SourceIdentifier (UPPERCASE) not rule name
   - code_desc format: 'config_rule_name: {name}, resource_type: {type}, resource_id: {id}'
   - Message (failed only): '{codeDesc}: {Annotation || default msg}'
   - run_time: ResultRecordedTime - ConfigRuleInvokedTime (seconds)
   - check description: include ARN, SourceIdentifier, InputParameters
   - source_location.ref: ConfigRuleArn

3. Source real fixtures from SAF CLI (~/repos/saf/test/sample_data/aws/) or heimdall2. The SAF CLI has aws_config_hdf.json (output) but we need the raw AWS API input format.

title: Design hdf-comparison schema (formal diff document type)
description:
Design and formalize the hdf-comparison JSON schema as a new HDF document type.

Research found no industry standard for structured security assessment comparison:
- SARIF annotates results inline, no standalone diff document
- RFC 6902 is structural only, no security semantics
- No security tool (Snyk, Grype, DefectDojo, etc.) has a public diff schema

This positions HDF as the first formal schema for security assessment comparison.

Key design elements:
- Terraform-inspired before/after snapshots (not patches)
- SARIF-compatible state vocabulary (new, unchanged, updated, absent, fixed, regressed)
- Configurable matching strategies with confidence scores
- 4 comparison modes: temporal, baseline, fleet, multiSource
- Drift vs changes separation (Terraform pattern)
- Multi-scanner conflict preservation (Automerge pattern)
- HDF integrity integration (signed diffs for audit trails)

Design doc: docs/plans/2026-03-13-hdf-diff-schema-design.md
close_reason: Schema designed and implemented

title: Add XML entity expansion DoS protection to Go XML converters
description:
HIGH security finding: All 11 Go XML converters use encoding/xml with defaults. Go's XML parser is safe from XXE (ignores external entities) but vulnerable to billion-laughs internal entity expansion causing OOM. CLI's 50MB input limit provides coarse defense but library use has no protection.

Converters affected: nessus, burpsuite, fortify, veracode, dbprotect, netsparker, xccdf-results, zap, junit, hdf-to-xml, nikto

Options:
1. Wrap xml.NewDecoder input in io.LimitReader
2. Document Go XML safety properties explicitly
3. Add entity expansion detection pre-check

The CLI readInputFile already limits to 50MB which bounds the worst case.

title: Fix double URL-encoding of project path in GitLab fetcher
description:
## Bug
When using `--project wdower/juice-shop` (namespace/path format), the GitLab fetcher returns 404. Numeric project IDs (`--project 1`) work fine.

## Root Cause
In `hdf-cli/internal/fetchers/gitlab.go`, line ~139-148: `url.PathEscape(f.params.ProjectID)` produces `wdower%2Fjuice-shop`, which is then assigned to `url.URL.Path`. When Go serializes the URL via `.String()`, it re-encodes the `%` to `%25`, producing `wdower%252Fjuice-shop` in the actual HTTP request. GitLab doesn't find that project ID, returns 404.

## Fix
Set both `url.URL.Path` (decoded) and `url.URL.RawPath` (pre-encoded) so Go preserves the intended encoding. Or construct the URL string directly without going through `url.URL`.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] `hdf fetch gitlab --project wdower/juice-shop ...` works (namespace/path format)
- [ ] `hdf fetch gitlab --project 1 ...` still works (numeric ID)
- [ ] Test added for namespace/path project IDs with slashes
- [ ] Existing fetcher tests still pass
close_reason: Fixed: URL double-encoding (RawPath), cross-platform glab config (adrg/xdg), hostname-with-port matching. Commit 90996ed.

title: Add --ca-cert and --insecure TLS flags to all API-based fetchers
description:
## Problem
None of our API-based fetchers (Splunk, SonarQube, GitLab, AWS Config) support custom CA certificates or insecure TLS bypass. SAF CLI didn't have this either. Users with internal instances behind self-signed or corporate CA certs cannot use live fetch mode.

## Requirements (12-factor CLI best practices)
1. **--ca-cert <path>** flag: Load a PEM CA bundle for custom certificate authorities (corporate PKI, mkcert, internal CAs)
2. **--insecure** flag: Skip TLS verification entirely (dev/test only, with a visible warning printed to stderr)
3. **Environment variable fallback**: Support HDF_CA_CERT and HDF_INSECURE env vars (12-factor: store config in the environment)
4. Implement once in shared fetcher infrastructure, not per-fetcher
5. AWS Config fetcher: wire through aws-sdk-go-v2 custom HTTP client

## Design Notes
- Go: Build a shared `NewHTTPClient(caCertPath string, insecure bool)` in `hdf-cli/internal/fetchers/shared.go` that returns a configured \*http.Client
- All fetchers call this instead of `&http.Client{}`
- --insecure should print a warning to stderr: 'WARNING: TLS certificate verification is disabled. This is insecure.'
- Cobra flags registered at the parent 'convert' command level so they apply to all fetchers
- TypeScript: Not needed immediately (CLI is Go-only), but if we add a TS fetcher layer later, use a custom https.Agent with `rejectUnauthorized: false` or `ca: [pemBuffer]`

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] `hdf convert splunk to hdf --live --ca-cert /path/to/ca.pem ...` works with custom CA
- [ ] `hdf convert gitlab to hdf --live --insecure ...` works with self-signed certs (prints warning)
- [ ] HDF_CA_CERT=/path/to/ca.pem hdf convert sonarqube to hdf --live ... works
- [ ] All fetcher tests still pass (no regression)
- [ ] --insecure prints visible warning to stderr
notes: [2026-03-03] Security review finding MED-4 confirms this need. Also fold in MED-2 (default to HTTPS-only, require --allow-insecure-http for plain HTTP fetcher connections to prevent token exposure).

title: Add ARF (Asset Reporting Format) support to XCCDF converter
description:
ARF (NIST IR 7694) is an XML wrapper format that packages one or more XCCDF TestResults along with asset metadata (IP, hostname, FQDN) and relationships. OpenSCAP and other SCAP scanners produce ARF as their primary output format.

The XCCDF converter should be extended to:
1. Detect whether input is raw XCCDF or ARF-wrapped XCCDF (root element is arf:asset-report-collection vs xccdf:Benchmark/TestResult)
2. If ARF: extract all arf:report elements containing xccdf:TestResult, extract asset metadata from arf:assets, and delegate each TestResult to existing XCCDF conversion logic
3. Produce a multi-baseline HDF output when multiple TestResults exist (one baseline per report)
4. Enrich HDF targets with ARF asset identification (IP addresses, MAC addresses, FQDN, hostname)
5. Register 'arf' as a CLI alias for the xccdf converter (similar to inspec-to-hdf aliasing legacyhdf)

Key ARF structure:
- Root: arf:asset-report-collection
- arf:report-requests — embeds or references the benchmark used
- arf:assets — computing-device with IP/MAC/FQDN/hostname
- arf:reports — contains one or more arf:report, each wrapping an xccdf:TestResult
- core:relationships — links reports to assets via arfvocab:isAbout

Schema: https://csrc.nist.gov/schema/asset-reporting-format/1.1/asset-reporting-format_1.1.0.xsd
Spec: https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/IR/nistir7694.pdf

The new findXmlValues utility from hdf-utilities is well-suited for traversing ARF's nested structure to locate TestResult elements and asset metadata.
close_reason: ARF support implemented in both Go and TypeScript converters, with format detection, CLI alias, and comprehensive tests. All 37 Go converter tests pass (28 XCCDF + 9 ARF), all 61 TypeScript tests pass (48 XCCDF + 13 ARF), all format detection tests pass, and CLI tests pass.

title: Implement format detection and routing in tool converters
description:
Tool converters (e.g. gosec-to-hdf) should detect the input format and delegate to shared format converters when appropriate.

## Design
Each tool converter's Convert function:
1. Runs format fingerprinting on input bytes (is it SARIF? JUnit XML? CycloneDX? native?)
2. If shared format → delegates to the shared format converter (e.g. sarif-to-hdf)
3. If native → uses tool-specific parsing
4. Optionally applies tool-specific enrichment after shared conversion

## Fingerprinting Heuristics
- SARIF: JSON with $schema containing "sarif" OR top-level version (string) + runs (array)
- JUnit XML: XML with <testsuites> or <testsuite> root element
- CycloneDX: JSON with bomFormat field OR XML with CycloneDX namespace
- XCCDF: XML with XCCDF namespace
- Native: tool-specific detection (e.g. gosec has GosecVersion + Issues fields)

## Shared format converter location
hdf-converters/formats/{sarif,junit,cyclonedx,xccdf}/{go,typescript}/

## Affected tool converters (SARIF-capable)
gosec, snyk, zap, jfrog-xray, fortify, veracode + any future tool that supports SARIF export

## Dependencies
- Requires enriched SARIF converter (comprehensive rules/relationships/suppressions/taxonomy parsing)
- Existing tool-specific converters continue working for native format input

---

## Progress
- [x] Format detection utility (Go + TypeScript) in shared/go/formatdetect.go, shared/typescript/formatdetect.ts
- [x] gosec converter routes SARIF input to shared SARIF converter (Go + TypeScript)
- [x] Tests: format detection unit tests (13 Go, 11 TS), gosec SARIF routing integration tests
- [ ] Other SARIF-capable tool converters (snyk, zap, jfrog-xray, etc.) — pending those converters being built

- Pointer helpers: sarif defines stringPtr/floatPtr, sonarqube defines stringPtr, aws-config defines ptr[T any] — should be one generic Ptr[T]()
- HTML tag stripping: nessus and sonarqube each define their own regex-based strip function
- RFC3339 multi-format timestamp parsing: aws-config, nessus, sonarqube each implement their own fallback parse loop
All four patterns are small enough to land in a single shared file with tests.

title: Audit converters for format-level commonality
description:
## Architecture Decision: Format-Level Routing

### Problem
Many security tools output multiple formats (native JSON, SARIF, SonarQube Generic, etc.). Users shouldn't need to know which converter to use — `hdf convert gosec to hdf` should work regardless of whether the input is gosec native JSON or gosec SARIF output.

### Decision: Strategy B — Rich shared format converters + tool-level format detection

Tool converters (e.g. gosec-to-hdf) become thin routing layers:
1. Detect what format the input is in (native JSON? SARIF? JUnit XML?)
2. If shared format → delegate to shared format converter
3. If native → use tool-specific parsing
4. Optionally apply tool-specific enrichment after shared conversion

### Shared Format Converters Needed
- **SARIF** (covers: gosec, snyk, zap, jfrog-xray, semgrep, CodeQL, trivy, checkov, ESLint, fortify, veracode)
- **JUnit XML** (covers: test frameworks, CI/CD outputs)
- **CycloneDX** (covers: SBOM tools — trivy, syft, snyk, cdxgen)
- **XCCDF** (covers: OpenSCAP, DISA STIGs)

### SARIF Converter Gaps (current → needed)
Current converter is minimal. Must add:
- `rules[]` definitions (name, description, helpUri)
- `rules[].relationships` → CWE taxonomy extraction
- `tool.driver.supportedTaxonomies` → CWE/OWASP awareness
- `result.suppressions[]` → notReviewed status with justification
- `rules[].properties` → confidence, tags, custom metadata
- `rules[].defaultConfiguration.level` → severity when result.level is absent
- Proper severity granularity from rule metadata

### Impact on Converter Count
- ~14 proprietary-only tools still need dedicated converters
- ~5-8 SARIF-capable tools can delegate to enriched SARIF converter
- 3 standard formats (JUnit, CycloneDX, XCCDF) get dedicated shared converters
- Net: fewer converters to build and maintain

### Format Detection
Use fingerprinting (check for `$schema`+`version`+`runs` for SARIF, `<testsuites>` for JUnit, `bomFormat` for CycloneDX, etc.) rather than requiring the user to specify format.

---
## Progress
- [x] SARIF converter enriched with full spec support (2026-02-21): rules[], relationships, taxonomies, suppressions, kind mapping, fixes, codeFlows, snippets, fingerprints, level fallback chain
- [ ] JUnit XML shared format converter
- [ ] CycloneDX shared format converter
- [ ] XCCDF shared format converter
close_reason: SARIF converter enriched with full 2.1.0 spec support. Remaining shared format converters (JUnit, CycloneDX, XCCDF) will be built as standalone tasks before individual tool converters.

title: Add junit-to-hdf converter
description: Implement a converter from JUnit XML test result format to HDF. JUnit XML is widely produced by test frameworks (pytest, Jest, Maven Surefire, etc.). Should include both Go and TypeScript implementations, CLI integration, and >90% test coverage per project standards.

title: Add inspec-to-hdf converter
description:
InSpec JSON output needs a dedicated converter for HDF v2. In v1, HDF was structurally derived from InSpec output format, so no converter was needed. In v2, a converter is required.

InSpec JSON output format: { platform: {...}, profiles: [ { name, version, title, controls: [ { id, title, desc, impact, refs, tags, results: [...] } ] } ] }

This format is the same as the legacyhdf-to-hdf converter input. The inspec-to-hdf converter should:
- Be a thin, well-named wrapper that clearly targets current InSpec output (v4/v5+)
- Set dataSource.name = 'Chef InSpec' and dataSource.version from the InSpec version field in output
- Handle multi-profile InSpec runs (one baseline per profile, or merged - TBD)
- Handle wrapper profiles (InSpec profiles that depend on other profiles)
- May share parsing logic with legacyhdf-to-hdf or may replace it once legacy migration is complete

Design question: should this share code with legacyhdf-to-hdf or be independent? The legacyhdf converter handles HDF v1 data that was already processed by Heimdall, which may differ slightly from raw InSpec output.
close_reason: Resolved via alias: InSpec exec-json is identical to HDF v1.0, so legacyhdf-to-hdf handles it. Added CLI alias (hdf convert inspec to hdf) in b1a1d8d and ubi9 STIG fixture in 686c001.

title: HDF schema: separate data-source from tool-creator in Generator
description:
The current Generator field conflates two distinct concepts: (1) the source tool that produced the original scan data (e.g. Nessus, gosec, SonarQube) and (2) the software that actually created the HDF file (e.g. hdf-converters, hdf-cli). Both need to be representable independently so consumers can determine provenance without inspecting converter internals.

Proposed change: split Generator into two fields or sub-fields:
- source (or dataSource): name/version of the original scanning tool
- converter (or creator): name/version of the HDF-producing tool

This is a schema-level change (hdf-schema) with downstream impact on:
- hdf-schema: TypeScript type definitions and JSON schema
- hdf-schema Go package: struct definitions
- hdf-validators: update validation rules for new/renamed fields
- hdf-converters (all converters, both Go and TypeScript): update Generator construction
- hdf-cli: update CLI version injection
- hdf-parsers: update any field references
- Possibly hdf-to-csv, hdf-to-xml output-side converters

Design questions to resolve before implementation:
- New top-level fields vs nested under existing Generator?
- Backwards compatibility: is the old Generator field deprecated or removed?
- Field names: source/converter, dataSource/creator, or something else?
- Version field: does each sub-field carry its own version, or shared?
- How should converters that have no meaningful 'source version' (e.g. static file import) populate the source field?
close_reason: Implemented as dataSource field on HdfResults (schema + all converters) in commits 7c2f694 and 1a4a878.

title: Implement SonarQube live fetch mode
description:
Add live API fetch mode to the SonarQube converter so users can run a single command instead of manually capturing the /api/issues/search response.

## What
hdf convert sonarqube to hdf --live --url https://sq.example.com --token TOKEN --project my-proj output.json

The fetcher lives in hdf-cli/internal/fetchers/sonarqube.go. It calls the SonarQube REST API (no extra Go deps — standard net/http), paginates /api/issues/search, and marshals the combined response into the same IssuesResponse format the file-based converter already reads. File-based mode continues to work unchanged.

## API mocking
Tests must not require a live SonarQube server. Use httptest.Server serving canned JSON responses pointed at via --url flag. Coordinate with hdf-libs-6b0.21.2 (Improve SonarQube testing without live server).

## Credentials / flags
--url (required), --token (required), --project (required), --branch (optional), --org (optional), --insecure (skip TLS verify)

title: hdf-cli: improve test coverage for stats and query gaps
description:
Mutation testing (Gremlins) identified two clusters of uncovered mutations in hdf-cli.

## Gap 1: stats.go — status counters (10 uncovered mutations, lines 84–90 and 174–180)
The `++` counter increments for `StatusError`, `StatusNotReviewed`, and `StatusSkipped` in both the global stats accumulator and the per-baseline breakdown are never exercised. Tests only create controls with `passed`/`failed`/`not_applicable` status.

**Fix**: Add test cases in `stats_test.go` that include controls with `error`, `not_reviewed`, and `skipped` result statuses and assert the counter values are non-zero.

## Gap 2: query.go — compareImpact operators (7 uncovered mutations, lines 329–333)
The `compareImpact` function has a switch over `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=`, `=` but tests only cover the equality case via `--impact` flag. The boundary comparison branches (`>0.5`, `>=0.7`, `<0.4`, `<=0.3`) are not tested.

**Fix**: Add `query_test.go` cases using each impact operator (`>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=`) and verify correct filtering.

## Other minor gaps
- `convert.go:87-89`: The error message branch for "both source and dest formats unrecognized" — add a test that uses two completely unknown format names and checks the error message contains the expected suggestion text.
- `list.go:177`: `truncateTitle` length edge case — test a title exactly at the max length boundary.

## Stryker config
`hdf-utilities/stryker.config.cjs` is in place for re-running. Use `gremlins unleash --timeout-coefficient 20` for Go.

## Resolution
Added to `stats_test.go`: `TestCalculateStats_AllStatuses` (unit, all 6 statuses via EffectiveStatus), `TestStatsCommand_AllStatuses_JSON` (integration, schema-valid result statuses covering notApplicable/notReviewed/error branches). Added to `query_test.go`: `TestQueryCommand_TextOutput_ImpactFilter` (exercises >, >=, < operators and the fmt.Printf text path), `TestQueryCommand_TextOutput_TitleTruncation` (56+ char title → `title[:52]+"..."`). Added to `convert_test.go`: `TestConvertCommand_ErrorMessages` (covers all 3 branches of `buildConverterNotFoundError`).

title: hdf-validators: update import assertions to 'with' syntax
description:
The `typescript/index.ts` file uses deprecated `assert { type: 'json' }` import attribute syntax (lines 5–12) for JSON schema imports. This should be updated to the modern `with { type: 'json' }` syntax.

## Why
- `assert` is deprecated in the ECMAScript spec; `with` is the current standard
- Stryker 9.x's Babel-based instrumenter cannot parse `assert { type: 'json' }` — this blocks mutation testing on hdf-validators entirely
- Updating unblocks Stryker and aligns with the current standard

## Changes Required
- `hdf-validators/typescript/index.ts`: change all `assert { type: 'json' }` → `with { type: 'json' }` on JSON schema imports
- Verify `pnpm test` still passes after the change
- Re-run `npx stryker run` with `hdf-validators/stryker.config.cjs` to confirm Stryker can now instrument the file

## Related
- Stryker config already exists at `hdf-validators/stryker.config.cjs`

## Resolution
All 9 `assert { type: 'json' }` import attributes changed to `with { type: 'json' }` in `hdf-validators/typescript/index.ts`. Pure syntax change; no logic affected.

title: Add bulk file operations to hdf-cli
description:
Enhance hdf-cli commands to process multiple files in a single invocation with summary reporting.

## Requirements

### Input Methods
- Multiple file arguments: `hdf validate file1.json file2.json file3.json`
- Glob patterns: `hdf validate scans/*.json` or `hdf validate "**/*-results.json"`

### Output Formats
- **Default**: Summary table showing per-file results
  ```
  Validating 10 files...
  ✓ scan-1.json         (results)
  ✓ scan-2.json         (results)
  ✗ scan-3.json         (results) - baselines[0].name: is required
  
  Results: 8/10 passed, 2 failed
  ```
- **--json**: JSON output for scripting/automation
- **--yaml**: YAML output as alternative structured format

### Error Handling
- Continue processing all files even if some fail
- Exit with non-zero code if ANY files fail
- Research and use correct GNU-style exit codes:
  - 0 = all files processed successfully
  - Non-zero = at least one file failed
  - Different codes for different failure types?

### Processing
- Sequential processing (not parallel)
- Progress indication for large batches

### Commands to Update
- `hdf validate` - validate multiple HDF files
- `hdf stats` - aggregate statistics across multiple files
- `hdf info` - show info for multiple files
- `hdf query` - query across multiple files
- `hdf list` - list requirements across multiple files
- ~~`hdf convert`~~ - skip (requires output file argument, complex)

## Implementation Notes

### File Expansion
- Need to handle glob patterns correctly
- Handle file not found errors gracefully
- Validate that globs match at least one file

### Exit Codes Research
Research proper GNU/POSIX exit codes:
- Standard: 0 = success, 1 = general error
- Consider: Different codes for validation vs I/O errors?
- Look at tools like: grep, find, ls for precedent

### Output Format Consistency

title: Review converter output for unnecessary null fields
description:
SYSTEMATIC REFACTOR: Nullable vs Optional Fields in HDF Schema

## Problem Statement
The HDF schema currently uses nullable patterns ("type": ["string", "null"]) for 123 fields across all schemas. This was originally intended to make fields optional, but in JSON Schema, nullable means "required to be present, but can have null value." This causes:
- Verbose output with explicit null values for unused fields
- Confusion about semantic intent
- Incompatibility with Go omitempty tags
- Wasted bytes in serialized JSON

## Current State
Total nullable fields: 123
- "type": ["type", "null"]" pattern: 96 fields
- "anyOf": [{$ref or type}, {"type": "null"}]" pattern: 27 fields

Distribution:
- common.schema.json: ~40 fields
- target.schema.json: ~50 fields
- result.schema.json: ~5 fields (runTime, resource, resourceId, message, exception, backtrace, status)
- hdf-results.schema.json: ~5 fields (depends, parentBaseline, description, inspecVersion, statusMessage)
- hdf-baseline.schema.json: ~2 fields (depends, remediation)
- extensions.schema.json: ~6 fields
- statistics.schema.json: ~7 fields
- platform.schema.json: ~1 field

## Observed Issues
From compliance.nessus conversion:
1. depends: null (1 occurrence at baseline level)
2. backtrace: null (5 occurrences at result level)

These should be omitted entirely when not provided.

## Root Cause
Schema design misunderstanding: nullable ≠ optional in JSON Schema.

For optional fields that can be omitted:
- DON'T: "type": ["string", "null"] with field not in required array
- DO: "type": "string" with field not in required array

The nullable pattern makes serializers include "field": null in output.

## Systematic Audit Plan

### Phase 1: Categorize All 123 Nullable Fields
For each field, determine:
1. Truly nullable (semantic difference between absent and null)
   - Example: status field where null = "not determined" vs absent = "not applicable"
2. Should be optional (no semantic difference, just omit when not present)
   - Metadata: title, description, version
   - Result details: backtrace, resource, resourceId, exception, message
   - Baseline metadata: depends, parentBaseline, statusMessage
3. Required with defaults (converters should always populate)

### Phase 2: Update Schemas (TDD Approach)
For each field categorized as "should be optional":
1. Update tests first to expect omission (not null)
2. Change schema:
   - "type": ["primitive", "null"] → "type": "primitive"
   - "anyOf": [{...}, {"type": "null"}] → {...}
3. Regenerate types from schema
4. Update helpers/converters to conditionally include fields
5. Verify tests pass

### Phase 3: Update Converters
For each converter (sarif-to-hdf, nessus-to-hdf, etc.):
- TypeScript: Conditional object construction (only add fields when present)
- Go: Verify omitempty tags work correctly after regeneration
- Update tests to verify omission behavior

### Phase 4: Documentation
- Document nullable vs optional distinction in schema README
- Add examples of when to use each pattern
- Update converter development guide

## Files to Audit
- hdf-schema/src/schemas/primitives/common.schema.json
- hdf-schema/src/schemas/primitives/target.schema.json
- hdf-schema/src/schemas/primitives/result.schema.json
- hdf-schema/src/schemas/primitives/extensions.schema.json
- hdf-schema/src/schemas/primitives/statistics.schema.json
- hdf-schema/src/schemas/primitives/platform.schema.json
- hdf-schema/src/schemas/hdf-results.schema.json
- hdf-schema/src/schemas/hdf-baseline.schema.json

## Expected Outcome
- Cleaner JSON output with no unnecessary null fields
- Clear semantic distinction between truly nullable and optional fields
- Better Go omitempty compatibility
- Smaller serialized JSON files
- Clearer schema intent for developers

## Priority
Medium - Not critical for functionality, but impacts:
- Data quality and readability
- Schema clarity and maintainability
- Output file size
- Developer experience

## Notes
- Start with depends and backtrace as proof-of-concept
- Most fields will likely become truly optional
- Few (if any) fields have true semantic need for null vs absent distinction
close_reason: Closed

title: hdf-parsers: improve mutation test coverage (36 survived, 38 no-cov)
description:
Stryker mutation testing scored hdf-parsers at **50.00%** (36 survived, 38 no-coverage) when run on unit tests only. Integration tests were excluded because Stryker's sandbox doesn't include sibling-package fixture files. Stryker config is at `hdf-parsers/stryker.config.cjs`.

## Root cause of low score
Most survivors and all no-coverage mutations are in code paths only exercised by `integration.test.ts`, which reads fixture files from `hdf-converters/converters/hdf-to-xml/fixtures/`. Stryker cannot reach these files from its `.stryker-tmp` sandbox.

## Cluster 1: Trailing-garbage detection (36 survived / uncovered)
`parseResults`, `parseBaseline`, and `autoDetect` all have:
```ts
const trimmedInput = jsonStr.trim();
// ... parse ...
if (serialized.length !== trimmedInput.length && !isWhitespaceEquivalent(serialized, trimmedInput)) {
  return { success: false, error: 'Input contains trailing data...' }
}
```
Every operator and boolean in this condition survived because unit tests don't include inputs with trailing garbage.

## Cluster 2: Schema validation failure path (3 survived)
`if (!validationResult.valid)` and the error message body survive — unit tests don't pass structurally invalid JSON (valid JSON, wrong HDF structure).

## Cluster 3: `autoDetect` type narrowing (4 survived)
`typeof data === 'object' && data !== null` and `'name' in obj && 'requirements' in obj` survive — unit tests don't call `autoDetect` with an object that lacks these keys.

## Cluster 4: `isWhitespaceEquivalent` (38 no-coverage)
Entire helper function never called by unit tests.

## Fix options
1. **Preferred**: Add unit tests that exercise the above paths directly — pass trailing-garbage JSON, invalid-schema JSON, and objects missing `name`/`requirements`. This avoids the sandbox issue entirely.
2. **Alternative**: Configure Stryker to include `hdf-converters` fixture files in its sandbox via `symlinkNodeModules: false` and a custom file pattern — complex, may break other things.

## Priority
Medium — the integration tests do cover these paths, so production correctness is verified. This is a test infrastructure gap, not a correctness gap.

title: hdf-mappings (TS): improve mutation test coverage (67 survived)
description:
Stryker mutation testing scored hdf-mappings at **72.48%** (67 survived, 187 killed). Stryker config is at `hdf-mappings/stryker.config.cjs`.

## Survived mutation clusters (affect all or most mapping files)

### 1. Lazy-initialization null checks (8 files × 2 mutations = ~16 survived)
Every mapping module has `if (mappings === null) { mappings = JSON.parse(readFileSync(...)) }`. Mutating to `if (true)` survives because tests always hit a warm cache — the cold-init path is never independently tested.

**Fix**: Add a test helper that resets the module-level cache variable to `null` between test runs, then assert the function still returns correct data after the reset.

### 2. `'utf-8'` encoding argument (8 files × 1 mutation = ~8 survived)
`readFileSync(path, 'utf-8')` — changing encoding to `""` survives because the test doesn't verify encoding was honored. With `""`, Node returns a Buffer; JSON.parse on a Buffer still works in most cases.

**Fix**: This is somewhat inherent to how Node handles encoding — consider accepting this survivor as a known false positive, or test with a file containing non-ASCII characters to distinguish Buffer vs string parsing.

### 3. Type guards `||` → `&&` (cci, nist, owasp — ~12 mutations)
Pattern: `if (!id || typeof id !== 'string')` — mutating `||` to `&&` survives because tests don't pass falsy non-string inputs (e.g., `null`, `0`, `false`). The `!id` check already handles those, so the `&&` mutation still rejects them.

**Fix**: Add tests that pass `null`, `undefined`, `0`, `false`, and `123` (number) to each lookup function and assert they return the correct empty/null/false result.

### 4. nikto `typeof id === 'number'` ternary (4 survived)
`src/nikto/index.ts:30` — the `typeof niktoId === 'number' ? String(niktoId) : niktoId` coercion is not tested with a numeric argument. Tests only pass strings.

**Fix**: Add a test that passes a numeric Nikto ID and verifies it's correctly coerced to a string for lookup.

### 5. nessus exact/wildcard match logic (several survived)
`src/nessus/index.ts` — the exact-match find predicate and wildcard fallback are weakly covered. The wildcard path (`pluginID === '*'`) is not covered at all (4 no-coverage mutations).

**Fix**: Add test cases for: (a) an exact plugin family + ID match, (b) a wildcard match (pluginID === '*'), (c) no match (returns undefined).

### 6. nist regex anchor (1 survived)
`src/nist/index.ts:105` — `/^([A-Z]{2})-/` anchor removal survives — the `^` start anchor isn't tested with a string that has a prefix before the NIST family code.

**Fix**: Test `getNISTFamily('prefix-AC-2')` and verify it returns the correct result (or no match if the regex requires start-of-string).

title: Integrate mutation testing into CI (scheduled / incremental)
description:
Mutation testing is now configured for all packages. This bead tracks integration into the CI pipeline.

## Tools installed
- **Go**: Gremlins (`~/go/bin/gremlins`, install: `go install github.com/go-gremlins/gremlins/cmd/gremlins@latest`)
- **TypeScript**: Stryker (`@stryker-mutator/core` + `@stryker-mutator/vitest-runner`)
- **Configs**: `stryker.config.cjs` exists in hdf-utilities, hdf-mappings, hdf-validators, hdf-parsers

## Recommended CI integration

### Option A: Scheduled nightly run (simplest)
Add a GitHub Actions workflow that runs on schedule:
```yaml
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 2 * * *'  # 2am daily
jobs:
  mutation:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-go@v5
      - run: go install github.com/go-gremlins/gremlins/cmd/gremlins@latest
      - run: pnpm install
      - run: pnpm build

      - run: cd hdf-cli && gremlins unleash --timeout-coefficient 20 --threshold-efficacy 100
      # Run stryker on TS packages
      - run: cd hdf-utilities && npx stryker run
```

### Option B: Incremental on PRs (more sophisticated)
- Gremlins: `gremlins unleash --diff main` — only tests mutations in lines changed vs main
- Stryker: `npx stryker run --incremental` — reuses previous results, only re-runs changed mutants
- Store incremental files as CI artifacts or commit them to the repo

- `pnpm lint` in pre-commit hook already gates commits; mutation testing is too slow for pre-commit
